summary:
Lunar Mission Browser is an interactive web prototype for exploring candidate locations near the lunar south pole and comparing mission conditions over time. It brings together solar illumination, Earth visibility, preliminary direct-to-Earth radio links, battery performance, data storage during communication outages, and terrain screening.

Users select locations, choose mission dates, configure requirements, and compare results through visual reports. NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data support terrain-aware calculations where coverage is available. NASA/JPL Horizons provides an independent ephemeris comparison, while Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap support map inspection.

Our main focus is communications: seeing Earth is not enough if terrain blocks the horizon, the radio link lacks margin, or the spacecraft runs out of power. By connecting these constraints, the tool helps users understand trade-offs before selecting a candidate site.

The prototype includes English and Spanish interfaces and a repeatable tutorial. It supports education and early mission studies, with explicit data coverage and model limitations; it does not certify landing safety or operational feasibility.
details:
Purpose and intended impact

Lunar Mission Browser helps users explore candidate lunar south pole locations and understand how illumination, communications, energy, and terrain interact. It is intended for education and preliminary mission studies, including scenarios relevant to Commercial Lunar Payload Services.

How it works

Users select up to eight candidate locations, choose a UTC analysis period, and configure mission requirements. The interface provides orbital and surface views, time playback, saved scenarios, and comparative reports. A repeatable tutorial explains the controls in English and Spanish.

Communications as a priority

The application distinguishes Earth visibility from a preliminary usable radio link. It evaluates geometric access, a configurable terrestrial station, radio link margin, and energy availability. It reports communication windows and interruptions and estimates how much data accumulates, is transmitted, or is lost when storage fills.

Illumination and energy

Solar geometry drives a configurable power model with panel orientation or ideal tracking, Sun–Moon distance scaling, battery capacity, charge and discharge efficiencies, and power limits. The reports identify energy deficits and their consequences for communications and data handling.

Terrain and NASA data

Numerical LRO/LOLA elevation data support terrain-horizon calculations up to 100 km around supported locations. A separate terrain-screening module calculates slope statistics, elevation range, and deviations from a fitted plane. It uses a processed 20 m grid around Shackleton or an 80 m regional grid where the complete study area is covered. Missing coverage and insufficient resolution are explicitly reported.

NASA Moon Trek supplies visual map context, LROC QuickMap supports external inspection, and NASA/JPL Horizons enables independent comparisons of astronomical coordinates. Numerical elevation data, visual textures, and shaded-relief images have distinct roles in the application.

Technical implementation and testing

The prototype uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Astronomy Engine. Terrain calculations use a lunar orientation table derived from NASA/JPL SPICE kernels. Scientific calculations run in a Web Worker. Automated tests cover geometry, energy conservation, communications, storage, terrain calculations, input validation, and data integrity. The current local version passes 94 automated tests.

Creative contribution

The project connects constraints that are often inspected separately. A location with favorable Earth visibility can still experience communication outages because of terrain, insufficient radio margin, or depleted batteries. Showing these relationships together helps users understand why a single visibility percentage cannot establish mission feasibility.

Current limitations and future work

This is an exploratory prototype, not an operational flight-planning or landing-certification system. Terrain coverage and resolution are limited. Small rocks, soil properties, landing dynamics, eclipses, partial solar-disk visibility, and detailed thermal or battery-aging effects are not modeled. Relay communications require orbit and service-availability data that have not yet been supplied. Comprehensive validation and full mission-report export remain planned work.

AI assistance

OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with software development, debugging, test creation, documentation, and explanatory text. External scientific datasets remain attributed to their original providers. Computed outputs are model estimates, not new NASA observations.
